'''''James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing''''' is a 2003 [[third-person shooter]] video game developed by [[Griptonite Games]] and published by [[Electronic Arts]] for the [[Game Boy Advance]]. As [[MI6]] agent [[James Bond]], the player must foil an ex-[[KGB]] agent who plans to use [[nanotechnology]] for world domination.

''Everything or Nothing'' was released in November 2003, a few months prior to the release of a [[James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing|home console version]]. It received "mixed or average" reviews according to [[Metacritic]].

==Gameplay==
''Everything or Nothing'' is primarily a [[third-person shooter]], played from an [[Isometric video game graphics|isometric]] perspective. The player controls [[MI6]] agent James Bond. [[Stealth game|Stealth]] is emphasized throughout the game, and several driving levels are also featured.<ref name=GS/><ref name=IGN/>

The game is divided into eight missions set around the world. On foot, the player has various weapons and gadgets to use against guard enemies who appear throughout the game. Weapons include guns, grenades, and land mines, and the player can also punch or kick. Medical kits are found throughout the game and are used to replenish the player's health. The player can take cover behind pillars or tables and can rappel down cliffs and buildings on some levels.<ref name=GS/><ref name=GSpy/><ref name=IGN/>

[[M (James Bond)|M]] and [[Q (James Bond)|Q]] appear after each level to brief the player. In each level, primary objectives must be completed before advancing. Optional secondary objectives are also present in each level, providing the player with Style Points if completed. At the end of each level, the player can use the accumulated Style Points to purchase armor, weapon upgrades, increased speed, and better aiming. A blackjack mini-game can also be unlocked by collecting Style Points. The player can sneak up on guards from behind and quietly take them out for additional points. A radar is used to detect enemy locations, and an alert meter tells the player whether they have been spotted.<ref name=GS/><ref name=GSpy/><ref name=IGN/>

The driving portions are played during certain missions and are also viewed from an isometric perspective. The player pursues a primary enemy vehicle and is also followed by several smaller enemy vehicles. The player's car has several weapons such as a machine gun, rockets, and oil slicks.<ref name=GS/><ref name=GSpy/>

The game offers a multiplayer [[deathmatch (video games)|deathmatch]] mode for up to four players, with the use of a [[Game Link Cable]]. A [[GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable]] can also be used to connect with the [[GameCube]] version of ''[[James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing|Everything or Nothing]]'', unlocking mini-games and upgraded gadgets, among other features.<ref name=GS/><ref name=GSpy/><ref name=GZ/><ref>{{cite web |last=Deci |first=T.J. |title=James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing |url=http://www.allgame.com/game.php?id=43564 |website=AllGame |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141114194832/http://www.allgame.com/game.php?id=43564 |archive-date=14 November 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Harris |first=Craig |title=The Ultimate List: Cube Connection |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2004/02/26/the-ultimate-list-cube-connection |website=IGN |access-date=16 September 2021 |date=26 February 2004 |archive-date=16 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210816023116/https://www.ign.com/articles/2004/02/26/the-ultimate-list-cube-connection |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Plot==
The game opens in the [[Sahara Desert]] in Egypt, where James Bond infiltrates and destroys a secret weapons facility. He is then sent to a casino in [[Cairo]], to investigate Arkady Yayakov, an ex-[[KGB]] agent and suspected smuggler. It is believed that Yayakov knows about recently stolen [[nanotechnology]]. Bond pursues Yayakov in a car chase, and his investigation leads him to a Cairo train yard that Yayakov had used as a shipping base. Bond discovers traces of the nanotechnology and also encounters a former foe, [[Jaws (James Bond)|Jaws]], whom he defeats in a battle.

MI6 learns that one of Yayakov's clients is an ex-KGB agent named Nikolai Diavolo, who has set up a base in the Peruvian jungle near a platinum mine. Bond meets with Agent 003, who has monitored the base, and they infiltrate the site. 003 is killed, and Bond pursues Diavolo in a car chase. He learns of another compound, hidden within a [[crypt]] in New Orleans. There, he discovers Diavolo is working with scientist Dr. Katya Nadanova. She has used a biological agent found in Louisiana to create [[nanobots]] that are capable of eating through metals, except platinum. Diavolo plans to unleash an army of platinum-coated super soldiers on the world while using the nanobots to destroy military defenses such as warships and tanks. He plans to initiate his plot in Moscow and intends to launch nanotech missiles to destroy cities unless his demands are met.

Bond escapes the New Orleans facility, and American agent Mya Starling is sent to destroy Diavolo's nanotech plant, located at the [[Andes Mountains]] in Peru. Bond is sent there after she goes missing, and he proceeds through the large facility, which extends underground through [[Incan ruins]]. Starling escapes, the facility is destroyed, and Bond travels to Moscow to foil Diavolo's plot. He pursues Nadanova's tank stops her, and subsequently fights against Jaws in another battle, before ultimately killing Diavolo.

==Development and release==
''Everything or Nothing'' was developed by [[Griptonite Games]].<ref name=PG/> The game features the likenesses of [[Pierce Brosnan]] (James Bond), [[Judi Dench]] (M), [[Willem Dafoe]] (Nikolai Diavolo),<ref name=GS/><ref>{{cite web |last=Goldstein |first=Hilary |title=James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing Hands-On |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2003/07/10/james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing-hands-on |website=IGN |access-date=16 September 2021 |date=9 July 2003 |archive-date=16 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210916145112/https://www.ign.com/articles/2003/07/10/james-bond-007-everything-or-nothing-hands-on |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Heidi Klum]] (Katya Nadanova),<ref name=GZ/> and [[Mýa]] (Mya Starling). Mýa also sings the game's [[Everything or Nothing (song)|eponymous song]], heard during the end credits.<ref name=GSpy/> The actors also provide minimal voice-over lines.<ref name=ND/> ''Everything or Nothing'' was published by [[Electronic Arts]] for [[Game Boy Advance]].<ref name=PG/> In North America, it was released on 17 November 2003, several months before the [[James Bond 007: Everything or Nothing|home console version]].<ref name=IGN/>

''Everything or Nothing'' received "mixed or average" reviews according to [[Metacritic]].<ref name=MC/> Critics generally found the game to be too short, with little replay value.<ref name=GS/><ref name=GSpy/><ref name=JXV/><ref name=XP/>

Frank Provo of ''[[GameSpot]]'' stated that the game adequately captured "the look and feel of a typical Bond film",<ref name=GS/> and Justin Speer of ''[[X-Play]]'' said the game has an "authentic Bond feel".<ref name=XP/> The on-foot gameplay was compared to ''[[Metal Gear: Ghost Babel|Metal Gear Solid]]'' for the [[Game Boy Color]].<ref name=GS/><ref name=IGN/><ref name=GPlanet/> Matt Helgeson, writing for ''[[Game Informer]]'', was critical of the isometric perspective: "It's sort of hard to plan your next move when you can only see about 10 virtual feet in front of you, and as a result it's usually easier to just run and gun your way through the levels".<ref name=GI/>

[[GameSpy]]'s Avi Fryman considered the game's environments to be "severely limited", writing, "There are few nooks and crannies to explore, few secrets to reveal, and few genuinely interactive objects".<ref name=GSpy/> Eduardo Zacarias of ''GameZone'' criticized the sluggish movements and the difficulty in aiming, and found the game somewhat repetitive.<ref name=GZ/> Other critics praised the gameplay.<ref name=GS/><ref name=IGN/> ''Nintendojo'' called the amount of variety "very admirable in today's heavily congested Game Boy Advance market".<ref name=ND/>

The driving portions were considered reminiscent of ''[[Spy Hunter]]'',<ref name=GS/><ref name=GZ/><ref name=IGN/><ref name=GPlanet/> with some negative comparisons by critics.<ref name=GI/><ref name=GSpy/><ref name=GMR/> Greg Orlando of ''[[GMR (magazine)|GMR]]'' called the driving portions "unwieldy and dull",<ref name=GMR/> and Speer also criticized the poor handling.<ref name=XP/> Fryman found this component of the game "not quite as fun or involved" as ''Spy Hunter''.<ref name=GSpy/> Conversely, Zacarias praised the driving portions and considered them "highly addictive".<ref name=GZ/>

The sound and music were praised.<ref name=GSpy/><ref name=GZ/><ref name=IGN/><ref name=XP/><ref name=ND/> Craig Harris of ''[[IGN]]'' opined that the audio is "where the game really shines", writing that the soundtrack is "outstanding" and "sets the mood perfectly".<ref name=IGN/> ''[[GamePro]]'' wrote that the soundtrack "really brings out the exhilaration of the espionage action".<ref name=GPro/> The graphics also received some praise.<ref name=GZ/><ref name=JXV/>
